Every single click, navigation, assertion, and API call in Playwright is asynchronous. JavaScript is a single-threaded language. It can only execute one line of code at a time. So, how does it handle a network request that takes 5 seconds to load, without freezing the entire browser and stopping all other code? --- Learning Objectives By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: - Use async and await. 1. The Restaurant Analogy (The Event Loop) Imagine a restaurant with only One Waiter (JavaScript's single thread). If the waiter takes your order, walks to the kitchen, and stands there staring at the chef for 20 minutes until your food is done... all the other customers in the restaurant will get angry and leave. That is "Synchronous" blocking behavior. Instead, the waiter hands the ticket to the kitchen (a background task), says "Let me know when this is done", and immediately walks back to the dining room to serve the next customer. When the kitchen rings the bell (The Event Loop), the waiter goes back to pick up the food. This is Asynchronous behavior. When JavaScript encounters an asynchronous operation (like fetching data or waiting for a Playwright element to appear), it offloads that task to the background APIs and continues executing the next line of code immediately. --- 2. Promises A Promise is the "ticket" the kitchen gave the waiter. It is an object representing the eventual completion (or failure) of an asynchronous operation. A Promise has 3 states: 1. Pending: The task is running in the background (The food is cooking). 2. Fulfilled (Resolved): The task completed successfully (The food is ready). 3. content: 1.3: Writing Assertions Learning Objectives By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: - Complete 1.3: Writing Assertions What is an Assertion? An assertion is a statement that you expect to be true. If it is true, the test passes. If it is false, the test fails and stops. In Playwright, assertions start with the function. The Essential 5 Assertions Playwright has dozens of assertions, but as a beginner, you only need these five to write 90% of your tests. 1. Verifies the text in the browser tab (the tag). 2. Verifies the current web address. 3. Verifies that an element actually exists on the page and isn't hidden by CSS (like ). 4. Verifies that an element contains exactly this text, and nothing else. 5. Verifies that an element contains this text, but allows other text to be there too. Auto-Retrying Playwright assertions are "smart." If you say , but the button takes 3 seconds to appear (maybe it's waiting for a network request), Playwright won't fail immediately. Instead, Playwright will keep checking over and over again, up to 5 seconds. If the button finally appears within that time, the test passes! This auto-retrying magic is why Playwright tests are so stable compared to older frameworks. It's also why you must always remember to put in front of . content: 14.1: Parallelization & Sharding State Pollution Avoidance [!NOTE] ?? Key Takeaway Parallelization distributes tests across local CPU cores (workers) on a single machine. Sharding distributes tests across entirely separate machines in the cloud for massive horizontal scaling. Learning Objectives By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: - Master worker-based execution Why Parallel Execution? Running 100 tests sequentially (one after another) might take 20 minutes. Running them in parallel across 4 workers can cut that to 5 minutes. At scale, this is the difference between a CI pipeline that gives fast feedback and one that blocks your team for half an hour. Each worker is completely isolated � separate browser, separate cookies, separate memory. Enter Fixtures Fixtures are Playwright's Dependency Injection system. Instead of manually creating objects (like ) inside every test, you simply declare what your test needs in the argument list. Playwright automatically creates it, passes it in, and destroys it after the test finishes. You've actually been using a fixture since Module 1: . You never wrote . You just asked for it: Playwright saw you asking for , so it spun up a browser, created a fresh context, created a blank tab, and handed you the object. When the test ended, Playwright closed the tab for you. The Magic of Custom Fixtures What if we could teach Playwright to do that with our own custom pages? Instead of this: We could write this: Wait, where did the login go? Playwright handles it automatically behind the scenes! By asking for , Playwright knows it needs to create an . Because if they tried to fill the input while the modal was still fading in, the test would crash with an error. This is called flakiness. If the computer is slow that day and the modal takes 3 seconds to animate, the test fails. Playwright's Auto-Waiting Playwright solves this entirely. In Playwright, you almost never write or manual waits. When you tell Playwright to click a button: Playwright does not immediately click the screen. Instead, it performs an Actionability Check. It rapidly checks a checklist under the hood: 1. Attached: Is the button in the DOM? 2. Visible: Is it actually visible (not or opacity 0)? 3. Stable: Has it stopped animating/moving? 4. Receives Events: Is it covered by another element (like a loading spinner overlay)? 5. Enabled: Is it not ? Playwright will sit there and patiently re-check this list over and over again, for up to 30 seconds. The exact millisecond all 5 checks pass, Playwright clicks the button. [!NOTE] 💡 Key Takeaway Playwright does not click immediately. It waits until the element is attached, visible, stable, clickable, and enabled. Trust the Framework Because of auto-waiting, you don't need to overthink synchronization for standard clicks and typing. If a test fails with a Timeout error, it means one of the Actionability checks never passed. Playwright will even tell you which one failed in the error message (e.g., "waiting for element to be visible"). [!WARNING] Never use (the Playwright version of ) to fix a flaky test! For example, you submit a form, and you want to wait for the "Success" banner to appear before checking its text. A beginner might try to write something like this: While exists, Playwright strongly discourages using it for verifying UI states. It makes the code verbose and harder to read. Web-First Assertions Instead of waiting for an element and then asserting on it, Playwright combines both concepts into Web-First Assertions. You already learned these in Module 1! When you write , Playwright does not check the screen once and instantly fail if it's not there. Playwright will auto-retry that assertion for up to 5 seconds. It sits in a loop: "Is it visible? No. Is it visible? No. Is it visible? YES." The moment it becomes visible, the assertion passes and the test continues. Assertions as Synchronization Points Because of this auto-retry behavior, you should use assertions as "synchronization points" in your tests. If you click a button that triggers a heavy 3-second database calculation, don't write . Instead, assert that the resulting UI state has changed! By using assertions to wait for the UI to update, your tests run exactly as fast as your application, without any arbitrary sleeps or flaky manual waits. --- Practice Exercise --- Common Mistakes - Hardcoding Waits: Using instead of waiting for an element's state. - Overly Broad Locators: Using generic CSS selectors like that might break if multiple buttons are added. Imagine a "Save" button that triggers an API call. 1. You click "Save". 2. A loading spinner appears. 3. The loading spinner disappears. 4. A green "Saved" toast notification appears. If the API is incredibly fast, the spinner might appear and disappear in 5 milliseconds—before Playwright even reaches line 2! The test will crash waiting for a spinner that already came and went. Waiting for the Network The most bulletproof way to synchronize a UI automation test is to stop looking at the UI and look at the underlying network traffic instead. When you click "Save", the browser sends a request. We can tell Playwright to wait for that specific HTTP request to finish! Why is this better? 1. Immune to UI Speed: It doesn't matter if the loading spinner was fast or slow. We only care that the server received the data and responded. 2. True Verification: Sometimes the UI says "Saved successfully" even if the API failed with a 500 error (due to a bug in the frontend code). By waiting for the network, we can verify the actual backend response. The Promise Pattern Notice the structure of the code above. We declare the promise before the action, and the promise after the action. If you put before clicking the button, the test will hang forever because nothing triggered the API call! Always set the trap, spring the trap, and then check what you caught. This pattern is the secret weapon of senior automation engineers. Playwright is not a browser tool—it is a Node.js library that sends instructions to a browser over a WebSocket (the Chrome DevTools Protocol). Because Node.js is single-threaded, it relies entirely on the Event Loop to handle multiple concurrent tasks (like waiting for a network request while clicking a button). When an SDET does not deeply understand the Event Loop, they write code that inadvertently fights it. --- 1. The Call Stack vs. The Microtask Queue When you execute a Playwright command: Here is exactly what happens under the hood: 1. The function is pushed onto the Call Stack. 2. Playwright serializes a JSON payload and sends it over the WebSocket to the browser. 3. The function returns a Promise indicating "I am waiting for the browser to reply." 4. Node.js moves the execution context OFF the call stack, freeing the thread to do other things. 5. When the browser replies "Click successful," the Promise resolves. 6. The callback attached to that Promise (the code after ) is placed into the Microtask Queue. 7. Once the Call Stack is empty, the Event Loop pulls the callback from the Microtask Queue and resumes execution. The Missing Disaster What happens if you forget the keyword? Because there are no keywords, Node.js fires all three commands down the WebSocket to the browser in the exact same millisecond. - The browser might receive the command before the command due to network jitter. - The test will evaluate the assertion before the login process has even started. Result: A test that passes 60% of the time and fails 40% of the time. This is the definition of flakiness. --- 2. The Trap in Data-Driven Testing
